title: Major Trauma, Haemorrhage & Thoracic Injury
note: Set 7: Learn chapters (Major Trauma, Haemorrhage & Thoracic Injury notes, structured for easy reading), learning outcomes, landmark trials and a linked reading list. Speak, Retrieve and SAQ content to follow.

items.title: 1. What is different about resuscitating a major trauma patient?
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P5 MINIMUM (2 parent LOs)
items.body:
- Major trauma is not simply an extreme version of routine emergency surgery.
- An injury mechanism produces simultaneous threats to airway patency, ventilation, oxygen delivery, brain and spinal cord perfusion, haemostasis, and thermoregulation.
- The priorities are therefore **to recognise and interrupt immediately fatal processes while organising definitive haemorrhage and injury control**.
- Diagnosis and treatment overlap: suspected tension pneumothorax is decompressed without waiting for radiology; a patient exsanguinating from an unstable pelvic ring receives a binder and blood while a pelvic control strategy is arranged.
- Conversely, transferring an unstable patient to CT may consume the time needed to stop bleeding.

- An often useful distinction is between **anatomical injury** (the lesion—splenic rupture, bronchial disruption, unstable pelvic ring) and **physiological injury** (the resulting haemorrhage, hypoxaemia, coagulopathy, cerebral ischaemia, acidosis or dysregulated inflammation).
- Successful care treats both.
- A patient may survive the initial haemorrhage but die from secondary brain injury, respiratory failure, sepsis or multiorgan dysfunction days later. [R01–R04]

## 1.1 Time-critical clinical priorities

- 1. Exsanguinating external haemorrhage (X): apply firm direct pressure, haemostatic dressings, a correctly tightened tourniquet for uncontrolled limb bleeding, or a pelvic binder where indicated. Do not let a prolonged airway discussion delay control of a readily compressible arterial bleed.
- 2. Airway with spinal protection (A): establish oxygenation and airway patency while limiting unnecessary cervical movement. Maintain a low threshold to call for an experienced airway clinician.
- 3. Breathing (B): immediately identify and treat tension pneumothorax, open pneumothorax, major haemothorax or tracheobronchial disruption; oxygenation may worsen dramatically after positive-pressure ventilation.
- 4. Circulation (C): find and stop bleeding and restore perfusion with warmed, balanced blood products rather than large volumes of crystalloid. Differentiate haemorrhagic from obstructive, cardiogenic and neurogenic shock.
- 5. Disability (D): record GCS component scores, pupils, limb movements and glucose; treat seizures and protect cerebral perfusion.
- 6. Exposure/environment (E): inspect the whole patient, prevent hypothermia, document wounds and burns, and plan a tertiary survey for initially missed injuries.

The primary survey is **repeated**, not completed once. After every intubation, transfer, chest intervention or transfusion decision, reassess relevant XABCDE elements. Deterioration is a prompt to re-search for haemorrhage, hypoventilation, a displaced tube, a new tension pneumothorax or a developing intracranial problem.

## 1.2 Preparing before arrival: the anaesthetist’s contribution

- A pre-alert should include age, mechanism and time of injury, suspected anatomical injuries, vital-sign trends, level of consciousness, oxygen/ventilation, drugs already administered, blood loss and tourniquet/binder placement, allergies and anticoagulant use where known, and estimated arrival.
- Use a standardised **ATMIST/MIST** handover: age, time, mechanism, injuries, signs and treatment.
- The mechanism is a risk clue, not a substitute for physiology: a high-energy deceleration injury raises suspicion for thoracic aortic damage, while a restrained crash may conceal significant abdominal injury despite initially modest vital-sign changes.

- Before arrival, the team leader allocates tasks and states explicit contingency plans.
- The anaesthetist verifies high-flow oxygen, functioning wide-bore suction, video/direct laryngoscopy, bougie, two second-generation supraglottic airway devices, capnography, emergency front-of-neck access, ventilator, in-line cervical assistance, and appropriately drawn induction/vasopressor drugs.
- Confirm IV/IO access equipment, arterial sampling, blood warmer/rapid infuser, the blood-bank contact and MHP activation process, calcium, TXA, warming measures, ultrasound, chest decompression kit, pelvic binder, tourniquets and ready access to theatre, interventional radiology, neurosurgery and transfer services. [R02, R05]

**Closed-loop communication prevents parallel tasks from becoming disconnected:**

- “Call blood bank, activate the major-haemorrhage pathway, return and confirm”
- “The right chest has absent breath sounds and the pressure is falling
- Prepare finger thoracostomy now.” The team should identify a single person responsible for repeated physiological summaries and major decisions, while delegating airway, external haemorrhage, ultrasound, access, documentation and family communication.
- A short pre-intubation pause when possible should include “What will kill this patient on induction?” and a plan for cardiovascular collapse or inability to oxygenate.

## 1.3 Secondary survey and the history that predicts severity

- Only once immediate threats are controlled, perform a head-to-toe inspection with an **AMPLE** history: allergies, medications (especially anticoagulants, antiplatelets, beta-blockers, insulin, steroids and recreational drugs), past history/pregnancy, last oral intake and events/environment.
- Record a defensible timeline for TXA eligibility, mechanism (blunt/penetrating, speed, occupant restraint, fall height, entrapment/crush duration), and prehospital physiology.
- Ask about chest pain, dyspnoea, limb numbness/weakness, pelvic pain, abdominal pain and an evolving neurologic deficit, recognizing that sedatives, intoxication, pain and shock impair reliability.

- The secondary survey includes scalp, face and oral cavity, neck, anterior/posterior chest, abdomen, pelvis and perineum, limbs and neurovascular state.
- Perform a careful log-roll only if necessary with adequate personnel; do not repeatedly spring/compress a suspected fractured pelvis to “test stability.” A **tertiary survey**, with repeat examination and review of imaging once awake or within ≈24 h as local practice permits, is essential for missed injuries such as long-bone, joint, spine, abdominal and peripheral nerve injuries.

### Mechanism-driven red flags and a genuinely complete secondary survey

- Mechanism changes the prior probability of injury and therefore the threshold for further examination, imaging and observation.
- A high-speed frontal deceleration raises concern for aortic injury, pulmonary contusion, bowel/mesenteric shear and cervical injury
- A lap-belt sign raises concern for small-bowel and lumbar flexion–distraction injury
- Lateral impact can produce pelvic-ring disruption and solid-organ injury
- Falls onto an outstretched hand may conceal cervical or shoulder injury in an older patient.
- Penetrating wounds require consideration of trajectory, number of wounds and multiple-cavity injuries rather than assuming the skin entry point defines the organ injured.
- The injury may also have occurred in a contaminated environment, changing tetanus and antibiotic decisions.

- Do not let a single ‘normal’ SBP override previous field trends.
- In children and young adults, tachycardia and vasoconstriction may preserve BP until a large fraction of circulating volume is lost; in an older patient receiving beta-blockers or with an implanted pacemaker, even substantial bleeding may not cause tachycardia.
- Anticoagulation, platelet inhibition, cirrhosis, pregnancy, frailty, chronic hypertension and baseline cognitive impairment all change the meaning of observations.
- Review prehospital haemoglobin if available but understand that an early haemoglobin may remain near normal during acute blood loss.

- A practical secondary survey documents a deliberate anterior and posterior chest inspection with palpation for rib tenderness, crepitus and unstable segments
- Abdominal peritonism, distension and seatbelt bruising
- Flank and back wounds
- Pelvic/perineal haemorrhage and urinary red flags
- Long-bone alignment, skin compromise, pain and compartment tension
- And distal motor, sensory and vascular findings before and after splinting.
- Record all wounds, log-roll only with an adequate team and a clear indication, and repeat examination when analgesia, intoxication or initial shock no longer make the patient unreliable.
- The tertiary survey should reconcile every imaging report, review devices and wounds, and ask the awake patient about focal pain or numbness overlooked during the resuscitation. [R02, R04]

items.title: 2. Why trauma physiology deteriorates so quickly
items.body:
## 2.1 Oxygen delivery, reserve and compensated shock

- Whole-body oxygen delivery is approximately **DO₂ = cardiac output × arterial oxygen content**, where arterial oxygen content is dominated by haemoglobin-bound oxygen: **CaO₂ ≈ (1.34 × Hb [g/dL] × SaO₂) + (0.003 × PaO₂ [mmHg])**.
- In acute haemorrhage, tissue oxygen delivery falls initially because stroke volume and cardiac output fall; the initial haemoglobin concentration may be normal until redistribution or fluid administration.
- Simultaneously, lung contusion, pneumothorax or airway obstruction may impair saturation, reducing CaO₂ further.
- The brain and heart have little tolerance for sustained combined hypotension and hypoxaemia.

- Sympathetic activation raises heart rate, contractility and systemic vascular resistance, preserving systolic blood pressure until compensatory reserve fails.
- Therefore **normal blood pressure does not exclude life-threatening haemorrhage**.
- Cool extremities, prolonged capillary refill, pallor, diaphoresis, altered mentation, tachypnoea, narrowing pulse pressure, reduced urine output and increasing shock index may precede hypotension.
- **Shock index = heart rate / systolic BP**; values near or above 1 in an adult raise concern, although age, beta-blockade, pain and pregnancy affect interpretation.

- Arterial or venous blood gas gives pH, base excess/deficit and lactate.
- Rising lactate and worsening base deficit suggest impaired perfusion but also reflect adrenergic stimulation, seizure, epinephrine, liver dysfunction and clearance changes.
- Look for the **trajectory after treatment**, not a single isolated measurement.
- Pulse oximetry and end-tidal CO₂ may become unreliable with profound shock; pulse pressure and ETCO₂ can nevertheless provide early signs of falling pulmonary blood flow after induction.

## 2.2 Differential diagnosis of shock in trauma

| **Mechanism** | **Pathophysiology** | **Clues that redirect management** |
|---|---|---|
| **Haemorrhagic (usually assume first)** | Loss of stressed venous volume → reduced preload and cardiac output; oxygen-carrying deficit | External bleeding, chest/abdomen/pelvis/long-bone injury, cool peripheries, positive FAST; no external blood does **not** exclude it |
| **Obstructive** | Impeded filling/forward flow | Tension pneumothorax (high airway pressures, unilateral signs), tamponade (penetrating chest, effusion; classic Beck triad unreliable), major PE (uncommon acute alternative) |
| **Cardiogenic** | Cardiac pump failure from contusion, coronary injury/ischaemia, dysrhythmia or structural damage | Arrhythmia, abnormal ECG/troponin, abnormal bedside echo, pulmonary oedema; can coexist with bleeding |
| **Neurogenic** | Loss of sympathetic vascular tone and cardiac accelerator fibres after high cord injury (often above T6) | Relative bradycardia, vasodilated/warm skin, hypotension; must exclude haemorrhage first |
| **Other/distributive** | Anaphylaxis, sepsis later, drug-related vasodilatation | Drug exposure, rash/bronchospasm, infective prodrome or chronic steroid deficiency; do not attribute shock to these without searching for bleeding |

- Haemorrhage can be hidden in the **chest, abdomen, retroperitoneum/pelvis, long-bone compartments and external environment**.
- A pelvic fracture may lose litres of blood without an immediately positive FAST because bleeding is often retroperitoneal.
- A bilateral femoral fracture may sequester a large volume.
- Hypotension after intubation can signify reduced venous return and sympathetic tone rather than “just induction drugs”; the response must include a fresh search for haemorrhage and obstructive thoracic pathology.

## 2.3 Trauma-induced coagulopathy and the lethal cycle

- Severe tissue injury and shock initiate endothelial dysfunction, glycocalyx shedding, protein C and inflammatory activation, platelet dysfunction, dysregulated fibrinolysis, hypofibrinogenaemia and impaired thrombin generation.
- Resuscitation can compound this with dilution, hypothermia and citrate-associated hypocalcaemia.
- **Temperature, pH, ionised calcium, fibrinogen, platelets and clotting factors are physiological components of haemostasis**, not laboratory trivia.
- Acidosis depresses clotting enzyme activity; hypothermia impairs platelet function and enzyme kinetics; ionised calcium supports fibrin polymerisation and myocardial contractility.
- This is often depicted as the **lethal triad** (acidosis–hypothermia–coagulopathy), with hypocalcaemia added as a fourth major derangement.

This pathophysiology explains why simply reaching a “normal BP” with litres of room-temperature saline can worsen haemostasis and mortality risk. The effective intervention is **early haemorrhage control plus warmed, proportionate blood-component resuscitation and repeated laboratory/viscoelastic review**. [R01, R03, R06]

items.title: 3. Airway, breathing and cervical-spine protection
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 3.1 When is a definitive airway needed?

- Intubation is indicated when airway patency or protection is threatened (blood, vomit, maxillofacial injury, burns/expanding neck haematoma), oxygenation or ventilation cannot be maintained, severe brain injury or seizures require controlled ventilation, or an unstable patient requires emergency surgery/transport during which airway loss would be catastrophic.
- A **GCS ≤8** is a useful trigger for assessing airway-protection needs, not a universally sufficient indication: it must be interpreted with airway reflexes, oxygenation, trajectory, ongoing seizure and procedural needs.
- Conversely, a patient with a rapidly enlarging neck haematoma and GCS 15 may require early intubation.

- The primary airway examination identifies blood or debris, mandible instability, facial fracture, trismus, penetrating/thermal injury, voice change, stridor, subcutaneous emphysema, aspiration and the potential for sudden loss of landmarks.
- Significant laryngeal/tracheal injury may worsen with conventional rapid-sequence intubation; a controlled spontaneous-ventilation strategy or bronchoscopic placement in an appropriately staffed setting may be preferable if physiology permits.
- Never assume a supraglottic airway protects against aspiration: it is a bridge if intubation fails. [R05]

## 3.2 Physiologically difficult trauma intubation

- The classic difficult airway focuses on anatomy; the critically injured patient also has a **physiologically difficult airway:** hypoxaemia, hypovolaemia, metabolic acidosis, possible right-heart dysfunction and raised ICP.
- Induction attenuates sympathetic vasoconstriction; positive-pressure ventilation increases intrathoracic pressure and reduces venous return.
- In profound haemorrhagic shock, a standard anaesthetic induction dose can precipitate cardiac arrest.
- Prepare a resuscitation and rescue plan rather than simply “using ketamine.”

**Before laryngoscopy:**

- Remove/loosen a rigid collar anteriorly if present, keep deliberate cervical alignment, provide two-person mask seal, suction rapidly, use head-up positioning where safely possible, correct treatable pneumothorax and haemorrhage, ensure blood is running if indicated, and prepare a push-dose vasopressor/rescue infusion while acknowledging vasopressors cannot replace circulating blood.
- Perform preoxygenation with a tight seal and PEEP if tolerated; consider nasal apnoeic oxygen.
- An early experienced first attempt using a video laryngoscope and appropriately shaped bougie/stylet is usually preferable to multiple traumatic attempts.
- If blood obscures the screen, suction and switch to direct view as needed.
- If unable to intubate, prioritise oxygenation, second-generation supraglottic rescue and an early **cannot-intubate/cannot-oxygenate** declaration followed by surgical front-of-neck access.

| **Drug or choice** | **Useful approximate adult considerations** | **Main risk/nuance** |
|---|---|---|
| **Ketamine** | Often ≈0.5–1.5 mg/kg IV for RSI, titrated to physiology; substantially lower in profound shock | May still cause hypotension in catecholamine-depleted shock; sympathomimetic response is not guaranteed; appropriate in TBI |
| **Etomidate** | ≈0.2–0.3 mg/kg IV where available | Haemodynamic stability does not correct hypovolaemia; adrenal suppression is a consideration, not a justification to delay necessary airway control |
| **Propofol** | Can be used in stable/appropriately resuscitated patients at carefully reduced dose | Marked vasodilatation and myocardial depression make full-dose use hazardous during active exsanguination |
| **Rocuronium** | ≈1.0–1.2 mg/kg IV for rapid intubating conditions | Prolonged paralysis hides neurological activity and requires sedation/analgesia thereafter |
| **Suxamethonium** | ≈1–1.5 mg/kg IV when appropriate | Avoid when denervation-related hyperkalaemia risk has developed after major burns/SCI/crush or neuromuscular disease; assess other contraindications |

- These are **typical educational dose ranges**, not a fixed prescription.
- In shock, dose and technique must be individualised and a profoundly unstable patient may need resuscitation before elective drug-facilitated intubation, provided oxygenation remains supportable.
- Avoid unrecognised **post-intubation awareness** by commencing adequate analgesia/sedation promptly; avoid avoidable hypotension.
- Confirm waveform capnography, bilateral air entry and tube position, but remember absent CO₂ during low flow can reflect arrest, not solely oesophageal placement. [R05]

### Induction as a haemodynamic intervention: preparation, choices and rescue

- Before inducing a shocked patient, predict how cardiac output will change after vasodilation and positive-pressure ventilation.
- A reasonable consultant-level verbal plan is: identify ongoing haemorrhage, request immediate blood and source control, ensure the team can decompress either chest, obtain IV or IO access, establish working suction and capnography, decide on oxygenation technique and the likelihood of failed laryngoscopy, and brief the team on the first vasopressor/resuscitation response if BP or ETCO₂ collapses.
- In patients with major facial injuries, intubation may become a surgical-airway problem; front-of-neck access equipment and a skilled operator must be ready, not merely somewhere in the hospital.

- Induction agents are titrated against shock severity rather than administered according to a standard elective weight-based regimen.
- Ketamine may maintain sympathetic tone in some patients but can still cause myocardial depression in catecholamine depletion.
- Etomidate has relative cardiovascular stability but potential adrenal-suppression issues; it is not mandatory or universally preferable.
- Propofol can produce profound vasodilatation in hypovolaemia and is generally reduced substantially or avoided in severe shock.
- Paralysis with rocuronium (commonly 1–1.2 mg/kg for RSI) or suxamethonium (commonly 1–1.5 mg/kg where appropriate) should follow patient-specific contraindications; for example, delayed denervation injury and major burns raise the subsequent hyperkalaemia risk of suxamethonium.
- Doses and agents should be chosen with a senior clinician, informed by age, mass, pregnancy, shock and airway factors, not copied from a memorised table.

- Preoxygenation deserves particular care when the patient is bleeding, aspirating or has a chest injury.
- Two-person seal and nasal oxygen may improve the available oxygen reserve, but NIV/PEEP may precipitate instability in marked hypovolaemia or an undrained tension pneumothorax.
- Manual in-line stabilisation and removal of the anterior collar during laryngoscopy allow access while reducing avoidable cervical movement; prioritise adequate first-pass conditions.
- The airway plan should explicitly cover contaminated optics (suction-assisted laryngoscopy, direct-view fallback), failed first attempt, rescue ventilation, and cannot-intubate/cannot-oxygenate front-of-neck access.
- Confirm sustained waveform CO₂ and chest movement, seek an ABG when the ETCO₂–PaCO₂ gradient may be wide, and maintain analgesia and sedation immediately after intubation.

- If hypotension or pulselessness develops, do not attribute everything to induction agent pharmacology.
- Reassess haemorrhage, tension pneumothorax, tube position, ventilator disconnection, cardiac tamponade and hyperkalaemia.
- Give appropriate blood and source control for haemorrhage; give titrated vasopressors as a bridge when required but recognise that an apparently corrected arterial pressure with inadequate circulating volume is not successful resuscitation. [R05]

## 3.3 Ventilation and perfusion after intubation

- For most critically injured adults, start lung-protective ventilation around **6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight**; individualise PEEP according to oxygenation, lung mechanics and haemodynamics, often starting low in ongoing haemorrhagic shock.
- Avoid excessive tidal volume/plateau pressure in contused lung, but also avoid high mean intrathoracic pressure when venous return is precarious.
- Aim for normal or near-normal PaCO₂, approximately **35–45 mmHg**, particularly in TBI.
- Routine aggressive hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction and can worsen cerebral ischaemia; transient rescue hyperventilation may be considered for impending herniation alongside definitive intervention.
- An arterial gas is more reliable than ETCO₂ for PaCO₂ when dead space is high or perfusion unstable.
- Avoid hypoxaemia; target an adequate SaO₂/PaO₂ rather than blindly pursuing maximal FiO₂ indefinitely.

**Post-intubation collapse algorithm:**

- Reassess airway/ETT depth and capnography
- Inspect ventilator/circuit obstruction
- Exclude tension pneumothorax, especially when unilateral breath sounds, high pressures or rapid hypotension occur
- Reassess ongoing haemorrhage, tamponade and cardiac function
- And promptly treat the most likely cause.
- With sudden arrest and compatible trauma, decompress a clinically suspected tension pneumothorax without delaying for imaging.

## 3.4 Spinal motion restriction and cervical clearance

- The objective is to minimise harmful movement of a truly unstable spine, **not** to rigidly immobilise every trauma patient indefinitely.
- Use selective spinal motion restriction: coordinated positioning, head blocks/manual stabilisation when needed, scoop stretcher or vacuum mattress for transfer, and careful lateral movement with adequate staff.
- Long boards are primarily extrication devices and should be removed once safe; prolonged pressure, respiratory restriction and raised ICP are avoidable harms.
- Rigid collars may worsen mouth opening and laryngoscopy, venous drainage and pressure injuries. [R07, R08]

- An alert, cooperative, non-intoxicated patient may be clinically cleared using a validated **NEXUS** or **Canadian C-spine Rule** pathway where locally adopted.
- NEXUS low-risk criteria require no midline tenderness, intoxication, altered alertness, focal neurological deficit or distracting injury.
- The Canadian rule mandates imaging for defined high-risk features (e.g., age ≥65, dangerous mechanism or extremity paraesthesia) and otherwise applies low-risk/active rotation steps.
- In adult patients who cannot be reliably examined, modern **high-quality multidetector CT** with multiplanar reconstruction is the primary test.
- Negative adequate CT can support collar removal even in an obtunded adult, following senior/local protocol.
- MRI or spine consultation remains appropriate for a focal neurological deficit, CT abnormality, radio-clinical discrepancy or concern for cord/ligamentous injury; do not simply clear an incompletely imaged patient.

## 3.5 NG and urinary catheters: small decisions with important consequences

- In severe facial or suspected anterior skull-base fracture, **avoid blind nasal instrumentation** (nasogastric tube and nasopharyngeal airway until injury assessed); an orogastric route is generally preferable for gastric decompression.
- For the urinary catheter, recognise blood at the urethral meatus, perineal/scrotal haematoma, suspected urethral disruption with pelvic fracture, high-riding prostate (unreliable sign) or inability to pass urine as red flags: **do not blindly force a urethral catheter**; request urethral imaging/urology assessment and consider suprapubic drainage when appropriate.
- A bladder injury does not automatically forbid every urethral catheter; define the mechanism and anatomical injury.

items.title: 4. Imaging during the resuscitation: choose a test that changes action
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
- Imaging is an extension of the primary survey, not an automatic step that every patient must complete before theatre.
- The central decision is **whether the patient is stable enough to leave a resuscitation-capable environment and whether imaging will change immediate haemorrhage control**.
- Unstable patients with a clear surgical target need control; CT is valuable in the patient who is haemodynamically stable or responding adequately to resuscitation.
- Do not confuse temporary normalization of systolic pressure after large-volume transfusion with physiological stability.

## 4.1 eFAST: what it answers and what it does not

- An extended Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma (eFAST) is a focused bedside assessment for **pericardial fluid, intraperitoneal free fluid, pneumothorax and pleural fluid**; it is not a comprehensive abdominal or thoracic examination.
- Standard windows include subxiphoid/subcostal cardiac, right upper quadrant (hepatorenal recess and inferior right pleura), left upper quadrant (splenorenal recess, left pleura) and suprapubic pelvic views, with bilateral anterior chest interrogation for sliding and posterior/lateral views for haemothorax when feasible. [R02, R09]

| **eFAST target** | **Expected positive findings** | **Important caveat** |
|---|---|---|
| Intraperitoneal haemorrhage | Anechoic fluid in Morison’s pouch, splenorenal recess or pelvic cul-de-sac | Early bleed, retroperitoneal/pelvic bleed, obesity and bowel gas can yield a negative examination; it does not identify exact bleeding organ |
| Haemopericardium | Pericardial fluid, and possibly signs of tamponade | Small/clotted blood or blood decompressing into pleural cavity can be missed; trauma physiology and mechanism remain vital |
| Pneumothorax | Absent lung sliding/B-lines, barcode/stratosphere pattern, lung point when present | Absent sliding is **not specific**: mainstem intubation, pleurodesis, apnoea or severe lung disease can mimic it; a lung point is more specific but not always present |
| Haemothorax | Fluid above diaphragm in dependent chest | Ultrasound describes fluid, not its source; confirm haemodynamic and surgical context |

- A **positive FAST in an unstable patient** with compatible mechanism strongly supports urgent operative control of intraperitoneal bleeding; a **negative FAST never excludes major haemorrhage**, especially retroperitoneal/pelvic or early bleeding.
- Repeated scanning can identify evolving fluid and haemodynamic response, but must not delay control.
- NICE specifically advises limiting imaging for unstable nonresponders to tests necessary to direct intervention, and not using FAST as a gatekeeper for CT in major trauma. [R02]

## 4.2 Portable radiography and CT

### How to interpret trauma imaging rather than merely order it

- A positive eFAST means that the focused sign is present, not that every conceivable injury is known.
- A positive right upper-quadrant view shows free fluid at the hepatorenal interface or adjacent pleural space, but cannot identify whether the fluid came from the liver, spleen or bowel; a negative view in early bleeding or obesity is insufficiently sensitive to exclude a major injury.
- In the left upper quadrant, examine the splenodiaphragmatic recess and inferior left hemithorax as well as the splenorenal interface.
- In the pelvis, the fluid pocket can be located posterior to the bladder or uterus; an empty bladder can degrade the view.
- Pericardial fluid on a subcostal or parasternal view prompts consideration of tamponade, but absent effusion does not fully exclude cardiac injury, and pericardial clot may be difficult to identify.

- On lung ultrasound, lung sliding and B-lines indicate pleural apposition at that exact site.
- The absence of sliding alone is NOT diagnostic of pneumothorax: mainstem intubation, pleural adhesions, apnoea, atelectasis and severe lung disease can also abolish it.
- A lung point is more specific for a pneumothorax when demonstrated, but may be absent in a large pneumothorax.
- Posterolateral dependent anechoic or heterogeneous pleural fluid suggests haemothorax, while consolidation and tissue-like lung are consistent with contusion or atelectasis.
- Septal movement and ventricular filling on focused cardiac ultrasound help differentiate severe hypovolaemia, tamponade and ventricular failure, but small hyperdynamic ventricles alone cannot quantify blood loss.
- All windows can be severely degraded by dressings, obesity, subcutaneous emphysema, external devices or operator inexperience.

- Know the difference between sensitivity (proportion of true disease detected) and specificity (proportion without disease correctly classified).
- Test performance changes between pericardial fluid, pleural air and small intraperitoneal collections; do not assign one ‘FAST accuracy’ to every application.
- A negative likelihood-changing test is not synonymous with a rule-out test.
- Repeat ultrasound if physiology evolves and escalate to CT or surgery when the clinical risk remains high.
- Its additional uses include identifying a large pericardial collection, assessing ventricular function, guiding access, and reassessing a chest after drainage; using ultrasound to guide a procedure does not make an unstable patient safe to delay for another scan.
- The 2022.2 examiner report singled out inadequate awareness of these limitations as a cause of lower marks.

Interpret the portable AP chest radiograph systematically:

- Confirm exposure and rotation.
- Tube position and lung inflation.
- Pleural air (including deep sulcus in supine films).
- Pleural opacity/large haemothorax.
- Parenchymal opacity/contusion or aspiration.
- Mediastinal abnormality and displaced trachea.
- Rib and clavicular fractures.
- Free intraperitoneal gas where visible.

- A widened mediastinum after blunt deceleration raises suspicion of aortic injury but is neither sensitive nor specific, and a normal film cannot exclude aortic rupture.
- On AP pelvic radiography, assess the pubic symphysis, pubic rami, iliac crests and sacroiliac joints, look for vertical displacement and asymmetry, and correlate with haemodynamic status and binder position.
- Pelvic radiographs may be avoided in stable patients going directly to adequate CT, but can identify catastrophic ring disruption rapidly during the primary survey.
- In stable patients, CT with appropriate intravenous contrast defines active extravasation, solid-organ injury and retroperitoneal bleeding; an unstable non-responder should not have treatment delayed simply to improve anatomical definition. [R02, R09]

- A rapid portable **chest radiograph** may show a large haemothorax, pneumothorax, mediastinal abnormality, flail segment or misplaced tube; sensitivity for occult pneumothorax and rib fractures is poor in the supine patient.
- A pelvic film may help identify major pelvic-ring disruption when CT is not immediately possible.
- In a stable adult with severe blunt trauma/multiple suspected injuries, **contrast-enhanced multidetector CT**, tailored to suspected injuries, reveals parenchymal, bowel/mesenteric, spinal, vascular and retroperitoneal lesions, with arterial-phase CTA for suspected aortic or major vascular injury.
- CT is particularly good at defining active contrast extravasation and selecting surgical versus endovascular treatment.
- Routine whole-body CT is **not recommended for all children**, in whom selective imaging minimises radiation. [R02, R10]

**Interpretation must be clinical:**

- A small splenic contrast blush in a stable patient with ready IR access can lead to embolisation; the same anatomical injury in a patient with persistent haemorrhagic shock may require urgent laparotomy.
- A widened mediastinum on CXR raises concern for aortic injury but lacks adequate sensitivity/specificity; CTA establishes the diagnosis.
- An “empty pelvis” on ultrasound does not clear a pelvic haematoma.
- Early CT can miss hollow viscus injury, so persistent abdominal pain, peritonism, unexplained lactate or deterioration requires reassessment.

items.title: 5. Life-threatening haemorrhage: resuscitation and control
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 5.1 Arrest the bleeding, then restore physiology

- Definitive haemostasis cannot be replaced by ever-increasing transfusion.
- Prioritise tourniquets/pressure for external bleeding, pelvic binder and temporary fixation for pelvic and long-bone injuries, chest drainage/operative intervention for massive thoracic bleeding, laparotomy or embolisation for intra-abdominal haemorrhage, and direct/endovascular repair for major vascular injury.
- The question is not merely “How much blood does this patient need?” but **“Where is the blood going, who can stop it, and what is the shortest path to control?”**

- **Damage-control surgery (DCS)** is an abbreviated operation chosen when prolonged definitive repair would be physiologically harmful—severe shock, ongoing bleeding, hypothermia, major acidosis/coagulopathy, complex vascular/visceral injury or severe competing injuries.
- First control haemorrhage and contamination rapidly (packing, temporary vascular shunts, stapling/resection without definitive anastomosis, temporary abdominal closure), restore physiology in ICU, and return for definitive repair when appropriate.
- This is not the correct default for every injured patient; unnecessary open abdomen and delayed surgery carry substantial complications. [R01]

## 5.2 Major-haemorrhage pathway (MHP) and blood components

- Early activation should be based on physiology and credible ongoing bleeding, **before** an arbitrary volume threshold is reached.
- Use local NZ/Australian MHP or Code Crimson when appropriate; communicate anticipated speed and amount of bleeding to blood bank, arrange immediately available uncrossmatched emergency RBC where needed, obtain group and screen/crossmatch, and liaise frequently with theatre and IR. [R03, R06]

- The initial phase uses a **balanced transfusion strategy**, typically red cells together with plasma and platelets at a high ratio rather than RBC alone.
- Many trauma systems use an approximately **1:1:1 plasma:platelets:RBC strategy**, with the practical convention that “one platelet unit” denotes an adult therapeutic dose; other systems use ≈1:1:2 or a fibrinogen-first, viscoelastic-guided strategy.
- These are treatment systems, not independently proven magical ratios.
- Australia’s NBA MHP guidance recommends in ratio-based protocols **no fewer than four units FFP and one adult platelet unit per eight RBC**—a minimum, not a target to prevent giving more haemostatic support if bleeding and coagulation results demand it.
- The PROPPR trial did not demonstrate lower overall mortality with 1:1:1 versus 1:1:2, but found earlier haemostasis and fewer deaths from exsanguination in the 1:1:1 group. [R03, R06, R11]

- Transition early from empirical ratios to **goal-directed therapy** according to haemorrhage, coagulation assays (INR/PT, APTT, Clauss fibrinogen, platelet count) and/or viscoelastic tests such as ROTEM/TEG, recognising that these tests cannot replace clinical assessment of actual bleeding.
- Samples should be repeated after interventions, ideally frequently during ongoing massive transfusion.
- Haemoglobin is lagging and should not be used as a sole trigger in uncontrolled haemorrhage.

| **Resuscitation issue** | **Useful specialist-level approach** | **Explanation and caveat** |
|---|---|---|
| **RBCs** | Give immediately for major ongoing haemorrhage; after haemostasis return to context-specific restrictive thresholds (often 70–80 g/L in otherwise stable adults) | A “normal” early Hb does not exclude life-threatening blood loss; haemorrhage is a dynamic physiological emergency |
| **Plasma / platelets** | Balanced early empiric delivery, then test-directed; consider platelets if <50 × 10⁹/L with major bleeding, higher (often ≈100 × 10⁹/L) in TBI/ongoing intracranial bleeding | Platelet dysfunction may precede count reduction; protocols and neurosurgical thresholds vary |
| **Fibrinogen** | Replace if ≤1.5 g/L or viscoelastic functional deficit in significant bleeding; an initial 3–4 g fibrinogen concentrate or equivalent cryoprecipitate may be used, then reassess | Fibrinogen falls early and is required for a stable fibrin clot; many centres aim >1.5–2.0 g/L during active bleeding |
| **Ionised calcium** | Measure repeatedly; aim within normal physiological range ≈1.1–1.3 mmol/L; correct promptly when low, especially during MHP | Citrate from blood binds calcium; low iCa impairs coagulation and myocardial contractility. 10 mL of 10% CaCl₂ contains ≈6.8 mmol calcium; 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate ≈2.2 mmol. Confirm local product concentration and access suitability |
| **Temperature / pH** | Warm patient, room, IV fluids and blood; prevent temperature <35–36 °C; correct ongoing shock rather than relying on bicarbonate to “fix” acidosis | Enzyme and platelet activity decline with cooling/acidosis, increasing bleeding; worsening metabolic acidosis is a marker of unresolved perfusion debt |
| **Anticoagulants** | Identify specific drug and last dose; reverse urgently for life-threatening bleeding using current local protocol and specialist advice | Warfarin typically four-factor PCC + IV vitamin K; dabigatran idarucizumab 5 g IV; factor-Xa inhibitors use protocol-specific strategies; heparin protamine. Antidote choice and dosing must reflect agent, time and thrombotic risk |

**Viscoelastic interpretation begins with the patient:**

- ROTEM EXTEM/TEG clot initiation prolongation can imply factor deficits; FIBTEM low amplitude implies fibrinogen deficiency; low clot firmness with preserved FIBTEM suggests platelet contribution; lysis signals hyperfibrinolysis.
- Responses depend on local instruments, reagent cutoffs and validated treatment algorithms.
- The 2025 ANZCA Blue Book on goal-directed bleeding management is a valuable specialist guide, but its algorithms must be reconciled to institution-specific reference ranges and available concentrates. [R12]

### From empirical MHP packs to a goal-directed physiological prescription

- A useful discipline is to reassess after each small batch of components or approximately every four red-cell units during major ongoing bleeding, recognising that the interval depends on speed of loss and local rapid testing.
- The Australian National Blood Authority guideline identifies temperature below 35 °C, pH below 7.2, base excess below −6, lactate above 4 mmol/L, ionised calcium below 1.0 mmol/L, INR above 1.5 and fibrinogen below 2.0 g/L as markers of critical physiological derangement; these are triggers for attention, not a complete set of automatic transfusion thresholds.
- The European trauma guideline uses fibrinogen ≤1.5 g/L (or VHA evidence of functional deficiency) as a replacement trigger, with an initial 3–4 g fibrinogen dose when appropriate.
- In actual care, treat active bleeding, VHA results and the institution’s MHP together; do not let the discrepancy between a ‘warning’ threshold and a ‘replacement’ threshold create delay. [R01, R03, R32]

- For clot initiation failure, consider factor deficiency and inadequate plasma, but also verify anticoagulants, heparin contamination and sample quality.
- For weak FIBTEM fibrin clot, replace fibrinogen using cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate according to the locally available product, rather than giving large volumes of plasma solely for fibrinogen.
- For low overall clot firmness with adequate fibrin contribution, examine platelet count/function and consider platelet treatment.
- Markedly shortened lysis indices or clinical hyperfibrinolysis may identify patients who need antifibrinolytic strategies, but TXA for eligible acute traumatic bleeding should not wait for a VHA trace.
- Remember that ROTEM/TEG values are device- and reagent-dependent; ‘A5’, ‘A10’, clotting time and conventional clot-strength parameters are not directly interchangeable and need the local validated algorithm.

- When using blood components, express both why and how much.
- The Australian/New Zealand guideline suggests FFP at a minimum one unit for two RBCs in a ratio protocol, an adult therapeutic platelet dose for approximately eight RBC units, and fibrinogen replacement of approximately 3–4 g when required.
- Because blood components and their labels differ between countries, do not equate an Australian cryoprecipitate unit with a New Zealand unit.
- The Australian guidance gives a New Zealand guide of roughly one unit of cryoprecipitate per 30 kg for a replacement dose; consult local blood-bank product specifications.
- Active significant haemorrhage is not the setting for a restrictive haemoglobin trigger copied from stable non-bleeding ICU trials.
- Once haemostasis is achieved, reassess haemoglobin according to oxygen delivery, brain injury and ongoing losses rather than continuing an empirical 1:1:1 strategy indefinitely. [R03, R32]

- Ionised calcium is a clinical treatment target because citrate-rich transfusion can produce hypocalcaemia and reduce contractility and clot formation.
- Monitor iCa repeatedly and replace in a titrated fashion according to the blood gas and local protocol.
- One 10-mL ampoule of 10% calcium chloride contains approximately 6.8 mmol elemental calcium and is best administered through an appropriate secure vein; 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate contains about 2.2 mmol elemental calcium and is less locally irritating.
- Choose agent, route and repeated dose according to urgency, line reliability, and iCa response.
- Do not assume identical doses in ‘10%’ ampoules.
- Also recheck potassium, temperature, pH, fibrinogen and platelets because transfusion and shock change these rapidly.
- Calcium administration cannot substitute for replacing depleted coagulation components. [R01, R32]

- Special circumstances deserve independent decisions.
- A known warfarin exposure with life-threatening bleeding may require four-factor PCC with IV vitamin K, with the PCC dose (often around 25–50 IU/kg) guided by INR and local reversal policy.
- Direct oral anticoagulants require identification of the agent, last dose, renal function, and available specific antidote or PCC strategy; seek haematology input while pursuing haemostasis.
- Consider urgent haemostatic radiology, surgery or direct vessel control alongside reversal.
- Whole blood may be available in some systems but should not be presumed universally available or superior in every setting.
- Laboratory normalization without control of a torn artery is not haemostasis. [R01, R03]

## 5.3 Tranexamic acid (TXA) and its evidence

- For a patient with significant traumatic haemorrhage, administer **TXA as early as possible within three hours of injury**, commonly **1 g IV over 10 min followed by 1 g over eight hours**.
- Do not delay for ROTEM confirmation.
- CRASH-2 found an overall reduction in mortality from bleeding, especially with earlier treatment; administration **after three hours** in patients with traumatic bleeding was associated with potential harm and is generally avoided.
- Seizures are a recognised exposure-related adverse effect at higher doses, and thrombosis risk must be considered. [R01, R13]

- The Australasian **PATCH-Trauma** trial (2023) asked a different question: in sophisticated trauma systems, did prehospital TXA improve survival with a favourable functional outcome at six months in patients at risk of trauma-induced coagulopathy?
- The primary outcome was not significantly improved, although survival patterns differed.
- This does **not** make TXA irrelevant; it means decisions should not claim proven long-term functional benefit, and care is still anchored in early haemorrhage control. [R14]

## 5.4 Permissive hypotension versus protected cerebral perfusion

- Before bleeding control, in an adult with major haemorrhage **without significant brain/spinal injury**, a lower-than-normal pressure may reduce ongoing haemorrhage and clot disruption: commonly a palpably perfusing central pulse or systolic BP roughly **80–90 mmHg**, provided the patient remains adequately conscious/perfused.
- This is a short bridge to control, **not an end point**.
- If TBI/SCI is suspected, avoid permissive hypotension: adequate cerebral and spinal perfusion takes priority.
- Brain Trauma Foundation thresholds to avoid hypotension in severe TBI include **SBP ≥100 mmHg for ages 50–69 and ≥110 mmHg for ages 15–49 or >70**, with a focus on sustained cerebral perfusion rather than a single reading.
- In pregnancy, elderly patients or those with cardiovascular disease, tailor the pressure to physiology and end-organ needs. [R01, R15]

**Do not treat hemorrhagic shock as vasoplegia.** Vasopressors can be used transiently to preserve essential organ perfusion at induction or in combined neurogenic/haemorrhagic shock while blood and haemorrhage control are established, but “correcting” BP with high-dose noradrenaline in an empty circulation can mask ongoing loss and worsen microvascular perfusion.

## 5.5 Point-of-care reassessment and when to stop the MHP

- Repeatedly assess external bleeding, surgical suction/drain outputs, haemodynamics, peripheral perfusion, ETCO₂, oxygenation, urinary output where interpretable, lactate/base deficit trend, haemoglobin/platelets/fibrinogen/coagulation, and ionised calcium/temperature.
- Communicate planned transfer and whether blood is actually arriving and flowing.
- Once bleeding is controlled and transfusion demand slows, **explicitly stand down the MHP** and continue test-guided replacement; leaving a rapid fixed-ratio MHP running causes avoidable transfusion and complications.

Transfusion complications include hypocalcaemia, hyperkalaemia or subsequent hypokalaemia, hypothermia, dilutional or consumptive coagulopathy, TRALI, TACO, haemolysis and infection. See Set 2 for full transfusion-reaction and anticoagulant pharmacology; here the emphasis is on decisions made in active trauma.

## 5.6 Resuscitative thoracotomy and REBOA

- **Emergency department resuscitative thoracotomy (EDRT)** is a highly selected last-resort intervention undertaken by a prepared trauma team.
- Its potential goals are to release tamponade, control intrathoracic haemorrhage, provide direct cardiac massage, treat cardiac wounds and temporarily cross-clamp the descending thoracic aorta to redirect flow to the brain/heart and reduce subdiaphragmatic haemorrhage.
- Best outcomes are generally in **penetrating thoracic injury with recent arrest and signs of life**, particularly tamponade.
- Outcomes are much worse after prolonged arrest and blunt trauma without signs of life.
- Policies differ in thresholds for witnessed arrest, duration and injury pattern; candidates must explain that patient selection, immediate surgical capability and rapid definitive control are prerequisites.
- Clamshell/bilateral or left anterolateral access and aortic control require trained personnel and large resources. [R16]

- **REBOA** temporarily inflates an intra-aortic balloon to restrict distal flow during noncompressible torso/pelvic haemorrhage.
- In an expert system it may bridge selected patients to definitive control, but it introduces ischaemia below the balloon, access injury, limb ischaemia and reperfusion problems, and can delay surgery.
- It is not a routine substitute for packing, direct surgery or angiographic embolisation, is generally not a solution to intrathoracic haemorrhage proximal to the balloon, and requires strict zone selection/occlusion times.
- **UK-REBOA** showed **54% 90-day mortality with a REBOA strategy versus 42% with standard care** (small 90-patient trial, uncertainty, possible harm).
- Therefore teach it as a conditional, resource-intensive bridge for selected patients, not a proven survival-improving standard. [R17]

### Selecting resuscitative thoracotomy in arrest: mechanism, physiology and resources

- The key decision is not whether a thoracotomy is technically possible but whether it has a plausible route to meaningful survival.
- EAST strongly supports emergency department thoracotomy in pulseless patients who had signs of life after penetrating thoracic injury; recommendations are conditional for penetrating trauma without signs of life or penetrating extrathoracic injury.
- After blunt injury with signs of life, benefit is much smaller and selection is highly restrictive.
- Blunt trauma without signs of life is a strong reason not to proceed, particularly with a long no-flow interval.
- Widely used time concepts, such as approximately 15 minutes of CPR for penetrating injury and approximately 10 minutes for blunt injury, are pragmatic selection aids, NOT stand-alone physiologic laws; local criteria and actual signs of life govern the decision. [R16]

- Signs of life can include pupillary response, spontaneous respirations or movement, measurable blood pressure or organized cardiac electrical activity, interpreted cautiously.
- A clinician must simultaneously treat reversible traumatic arrest causes: oxygenation, haemorrhage control, pelvic binder, bilateral chest decompression when indicated, and a coordinated transfusion response.
- Resuscitative thoracotomy may decompress tamponade, allow direct repair of a penetrating cardiac injury, provide internal cardiac massage and permit temporary descending aortic clamping to preserve proximal perfusion; it will not repair uncontrolled bleeding from multiple major compartments by itself.
- Aortic occlusion rapidly compromises abdominal organ and lower-limb flow, so a definitive surgical pathway must already be identified.
- The anaesthetist coordinates blood products, warming, ventilator/airway support, analgesia/sedation in patients with signs of life, and communication of cessation criteria. [R16]

- For REBOA, describe the anatomy in addition to the evidence.
- Proximal zone I occlusion may bridge catastrophic subdiaphragmatic haemorrhage; zone III may be selected for isolated pelvic haemorrhage in a patient without major abdominal bleeding; zone II is avoided.
- Balloon occlusion is temporary, and longer occlusion substantially increases ischaemia, reperfusion acidosis, limb injury and organ failure.
- Balloon placement requires skilled arterial access, rapid access to theatre or IR and immediate plans for deflation, haemorrhage control and reperfusion; it is inappropriate to use it simply because there is a femoral introducer available.
- UK-REBOA found numerically higher 90-day mortality with the REBOA strategy and did not demonstrate a survival benefit. [R17]

items.body:
## 6.1 Why chest injury kills

- Traumatic respiratory failure may result from **mechanical failure** (rib fractures/flail segment and pain limiting tidal volume), **loss of aerated lung** (pneumothorax/haemothorax), **gas-exchange injury** (pulmonary contusion/aspiration/ARDS), **airway interruption** (laryngotracheal disruption, bronchopleural fistula), or **circulatory obstruction/haemorrhage** (tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, aortic or pulmonary vascular injury).
- These processes often coexist, so persistent hypoxaemia after treating a pneumothorax is not evidence of procedural failure: a pulmonary contusion or aspiration may remain. [R09, R18]

The differential diagnosis of **hypoxia in the trauma patient** should be deliberately broad:

- Upper airway obstruction, endotracheal tube obstruction/displacement/mainstem placement, inadequate ventilation or drug effect.
- Pneumothorax or tension pneumothorax.
- Haemothorax.
- Pulmonary contusion/ARDS.
- Aspiration.
- Atelectasis from pain or sedation.
- Flail chest.
- Severe bronchospasm, underlying COPD.
- Tracheobronchial injury with air leak.
- Pulmonary embolism/fat embolism later.
- Shock and reduced mixed venous oxygen content.
- Equipment failure.

- A rapidly worsening SpO₂ with high ventilator pressure and falling BP immediately after induction makes **tension pneumothorax** a high-stakes diagnosis.
- Re-evaluate with inspection, auscultation, capnography, airway pressure, focused ultrasound and immediate clinical intervention rather than relying on a single sign.

## 6.2 Pneumothorax and tension physiology

- Air entering the pleural cavity reduces negative transpulmonary distending pressure, causing ipsilateral lung collapse and intrapulmonary shunt.
- With progressive one-way air entry under positive pressure, intrathoracic pressure rises, compressing great veins and impairing venous return; the result is **obstructive shock**.
- Classical distended neck veins, tracheal shift and hyperresonance may be absent, especially in hypovolaemia, obesity or noisy resuscitation environments.
- An awake patient may have unilateral pleuritic pain, tachypnoea, hypoxaemia and reduced breath sounds.
- In an intubated patient, look for sudden elevated airway pressure, falling oxygen saturation, hypotension, reduced ETCO₂ and unilateral reduced air entry.

- A **suspected tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis:** decompress immediately without waiting for CXR or CT.
- In a ventilated trauma patient with skilled personnel, **finger thoracostomy in the fourth or fifth intercostal space in the lateral safe-triangle region** followed by definitive intercostal drain is often preferred; needle decompression remains a temporising alternative where finger access cannot immediately be performed and can fail from inadequate length or kinking.
- Once decompressed, secure appropriate drainage and reassess oxygenation and circulation. [R18, R19]

- A small pneumothorax in a stable spontaneously breathing patient can sometimes be observed with repeat imaging and access to rescue drainage.
- In patients with positive-pressure ventilation, ongoing respiratory compromise, worsening size or haemodynamic impact, drainage is usually indicated; very small occult pneumothoraces can sometimes be observed during low-pressure ventilation in specialist settings with immediate rescue capability.
- There is no universally correct “all positive-pressure ventilation requires a drain” rule; severity, site, planned surgery and risk of delayed tension matter.

## 6.3 Technique: emergency finger thoracostomy

**Preparation and site:**

- Rapidly identify the fourth–fifth interspace, around the anterior/mid-axillary line within the safe triangle, choosing a site above a rib to protect the intercostal neurovascular bundle running beneath the rib.
- Use asepsis and local anaesthetic when time permits, but do not delay a lifesaving intervention in arrest or pre-arrest.
- For a profoundly unstable patient with bilateral suspected tension pathology (e.g. traumatic arrest), bilateral thoracic decompression may be appropriate within the resuscitation protocol.

**Procedure:**

- Make an adequately long skin incision along the interspace
- Dissect bluntly through muscle over the upper border of the lower rib
- Open the pleura with a curved clamp
- Insert a gloved finger to confirm entry, open pleural space and exclude adhesions or adjacent organ
- Release air/blood.
- Follow with an intercostal catheter secured to an underwater-seal system.
- Immediate improvement in BP/ETCO₂ and breath sounds is supportive but not proof that every pathology has been treated.
- Inadequate depth, wrong site, diaphragm or abdominal injury, intercostal vessel laceration and failed skin–pleura communication are important complications.

## 6.4 Intercostal catheter insertion and management

- Chest-drain placement is a full procedure with consent if possible, monitoring, analgesia, sterile conditions and haemorrhage preparations.
- Common trauma placement is around **fourth–fifth intercostal space in the safe triangle**; blunt dissection above the rib and finger confirmation are safer than blind trocar insertion.
- A drain is directed to achieve drainage of the clinically relevant air/fluid, connected to an underwater seal and secured with appropriate fixation/occlusive dressing.
- Confirm side, position, function, output and lung re-expansion with imaging where appropriate; document initial and subsequent blood drainage.

- For significant traumatic haemothorax, adequately sized drains that resist clot blockage are customary; **24–32 Fr** are often used, but modern data allow smaller catheters in selected stable patients.
- Unstable massive haemothorax needs immediate operative assessment, not a debate about French size.
- Low-bore devices may be appropriate for selected pneumothoraces, while small isolated pneumothoraces may sometimes be managed without a tube.
- Avoid creating suction-related air leaks, monitor tube patency, and do not clamp a bubbling drain without an explicit expert indication.
- Risks include organ and diaphragm injury, intercostal bleeding, infection/empyema, pain, subcutaneous placement and retained haemothorax. [R09]

### Chest-drain troubleshooting, safe removal and the observation decision

- The distinction between a stable small collection and an unstable chest injury is fundamental.
- The 2025 WSES–AAST guideline supports observation with close reassessment for selected stable small pneumothoraces (approximately ≤2 cm by its described imaging assessment) and small haemothoraces (less than about 300 mL), with at least 24 hours’ observation for an occult small pneumothorax.
- It recommends drainage of a haemothorax approximately ≥500 mL and urgent large-bore drainage in unstable patients regardless of estimated size.
- Clinical deterioration, positive-pressure ventilation, associated injuries, transport and access to immediate decompression can make observation unsafe even when a scan looks small.
- These cutoffs cannot replace trauma-team judgement. [R09]

- Drain size and access should match the indication: a small-bore drain may be appropriate for selected stable pneumothoraces, while active large haemothorax with clot is commonly managed with 28–32 Fr or similar large-bore drainage.
- Identify the diaphragm and the safe triangle before incision, enter above the rib, and confirm the pleural space by finger, not blind trocar thrusting.
- Document the starting blood volume, serial output, air leak and degree of lung expansion.
- If a drain stops bubbling or stops draining, this might indicate resolution, malposition, kinking, obstruction or complete disconnection—inspect the patient first and never interpret a quiet chamber in isolation.
- A new continuous large air leak with poor lung expansion raises concern for bronchial injury or a damaged drainage circuit; clamp only under an explicit senior plan because clamping an active air leak can precipitate tension pneumothorax.

- A sudden collapse after chest-drain insertion has several critical explanations: additional bleeding from a damaged intercostal or internal mammary vessel, drainage of a previously tamponaded vascular injury, deterioration of a tension pneumothorax through failed drainage, vagal event, acute re-expansion pulmonary oedema or an unrelated evolving injury.
- Reassess XABCDE immediately and seek surgical help.
- If the tube was inadvertently placed into lung, liver or spleen, do not blindly remove it: leave it secured and obtain urgent imaging and coordinated surgical management.
- Prophylactic antibiotics are not routine for uncomplicated blunt pneumothorax drainage but are appropriate with penetrating/open thoracic injuries according to local policy; established empyema is a separate therapeutic problem.
- Once leak has resolved, drainage is minimal, and imaging/clinical findings show re-expansion, consider removal according to local suction/water-seal protocols with an observed post-removal plan. [R09]

## 6.5 Haemothorax and thoracotomy thresholds

- A haemothorax reduces ventilated lung volume and simultaneously removes circulating blood.
- Chest tube drainage both treats physiological compromise and **quantifies ongoing bleeding**, but a clotted or poorly positioned tube can underestimate blood loss.
- Suspect intercostal, internal mammary, pulmonary parenchymal or major vascular injury.
- Establish blood transfusion and haemorrhage control concurrently.
- Common triggers to consider urgent thoracotomy include approximately **≥1.5 L immediately drained**, or sustained **>200 mL/h over several hours**, especially with ongoing instability or transfusion requirement.
- These are guides: a patient with lower measured output but persistent shock and a large retained collection may need surgery; a transient high initial volume followed by stability is interpreted in the full context. [R09]

Retained haemothorax predisposes to infection, empyema and fibrothorax. Stable patients with significant retained clot may need early video-assisted thoracoscopic evacuation rather than simply prolonged tube dwell. In unstable massive bleeding, definitive thoracic surgery takes priority.

### Large and retained haemothorax: blood loss, infection and operative decisions

- Quantification helps but must not obscure ongoing physiology.
- The 2025 WSES–AAST guideline suggests operative consideration with haemodynamic instability due to thoracic bleeding, initial or cumulative drainage consistent with major loss (often >1.5 L), or ongoing drainage >200 mL/h over three successive hours.
- Haemorrhage into an undrained or clotted pleural space can be underestimated by a reassuring drain chart.
- If the patient remains shocked, re-examine for other bleeding compartments while considering emergency thoracic surgical control.
- Chest tube drainage is treatment of pleural physiology and measurement of bleeding; it is not definitive repair of a torn intercostal, mammary or great vessel. [R09]

- A persistent opacity despite apparently working drainage should trigger consideration of retained haemothorax, especially with fever, leukocytosis, hypoxaemia or failure of lung expansion.
- CT helps distinguish clot, lung contusion and compressive atelectasis in a stable patient.
- Early VATS, often within a few days when feasible, may reduce later empyema/fibrothorax and avoids repeated blind tube manipulation; late organised clots can require decortication.
- Give timely antibiotics and drain an established infected collection, but do not give prophylactic antibiotics merely because a patient has pulmonary contusion.
- After evacuation reassess ventilation, analgesia, chest drain function, infection and subsequent mobilisation. [R09]

## 6.6 Rib fractures, flail chest and pulmonary contusion

- Fractured ribs cause splinting: shallow breathing → impaired cough → atelectasis and secretion retention → pneumonia and worsening hypoxaemia.
- Elderly patients, those with COPD/frailty, multiple displaced ribs, bilateral injury or associated pulmonary contusion deteriorate particularly readily.
- Importantly, a radiograph may **miss many rib fractures**, and early low-risk vital signs do not exclude a severe pulmonary contusion.
- Assess the ability to cough, deep breathe and mobilise, oxygen demand, pain at rest and movement, incentive spirometry if used locally, trajectory and frailty; scores such as STUMBL may support but not replace clinical judgement. [R20, R21]

- A **flail segment** classically results from three or more contiguous ribs fractured at two or more sites (or an equivalent unstable chest-wall segment).
- Paradoxical chest movement can occur, but respiratory failure more often reflects combined pain, contused lung and abnormal mechanics rather than paradox alone.
- Initial treatment provides adequate analgesia, oxygen, chest physiotherapy, secretion clearance and lung-protective ventilation if needed.
- NIV/HFNO may help a cooperative stable patient but are hazardous if an undrained significant pneumothorax, impaired airway protection, vomiting or unstable shock is present.

- **Pulmonary contusion** is alveolar/interstitial haemorrhage and oedema without major laceration.
- Impaired diffusion, increased shunt, reduced compliance and inflammatory lung injury may evolve during the first **24–48 h**.
- Avoid excessive crystalloid, particularly after haemorrhage control; this is not a recommendation to under-resuscitate shock.
- Use appropriate oxygenation support, pain relief, physiotherapy and protective ventilation; do not give prophylactic antibiotics or steroids simply for uncomplicated contusion.
- Vigilance for aspiration, pneumonia, ARDS and delayed respiratory failure is important. [R09, R20]

## 6.7 Surgical stabilisation of rib fractures (SSRF)

- Fixation may improve chest-wall mechanics and reduce ventilator days or pulmonary complications in selected patients.
- The **2025 WSES-AAST guidance** recommends considering SSRF in stable patients with flail chest, and also in selected patients with **≥3 ipsilateral severely displaced ribs**, failed ventilator weaning or uncontrolled pain despite optimal care.
- When feasible, treatment within **48–72 h** is preferred; if early surgery is unsuitable, consideration within **3–7 days** may still be valuable.
- **Haemodynamic instability is a contraindication** until resuscitated; pulmonary contusion or TBI are not automatically absolute contraindications. [R09, R22]

- Anaesthetic planning must account for lung contusion, coexisting injuries, anticoagulation, positioning, possible one-lung ventilation, surgical duration, temperature and postoperative analgesia.
- A double-lumen tube or bronchial blocker may be needed for surgical access, but it should not be used reflexively if oxygenation is marginal.
- Choose the simplest safe technique consistent with surgical exposure.
- Regional catheter placement before or after fixation can facilitate extubation.

### Rib-fracture risk and postoperative fixation decisions

- For risk stratification, interpret anatomy and physiology together: the number of ribs, displacement, bilateral fractures, radiographic flail segment, pulmonary contusion, age, frailty, COPD, oxygen requirement, cough and incentive spirometry predict different elements of deterioration.
- A weak cough and a falling inspiratory capacity despite acceptable resting saturation can be a more actionable warning than an isolated normal arterial gas.
- Scores such as STUMBL or regional pathways are aids to escalation, not substitutes for repeat assessment.
- The NZ RIB-IMPROVE experience illustrates the benefits of standardised admission review, analgesia escalation and physiotherapy in real hospital pathways. [R20, R21, R33]

- Flail chest is a clinical paradoxical-motion syndrome, while a radiographic flail segment can exist without obvious paradox if pain and surrounding tissues splint the segment.
- The primary problems are lung contusion, splinting, atelectasis and respiratory work; routine intubation solely because a flail segment exists is not necessary if gas exchange and work of breathing are adequate.
- When repair is selected, the trauma anaesthetist should provide a specific plan for OLV need versus two-lung ventilation, management of associated pleural collections, lung-protective strategies, and catheter-based analgesia; severe pain persisting after fixation may indicate nerve injury or associated pathology.
- Evidence most consistently supports reductions in ventilation duration, pneumonia and ICU length of stay in suitable patients, not a universal mortality benefit.
- The 2024 WSES/CWIS position paper and 2025 WSES–AAST guideline recommend considering early fixation within 48–72 h in suitable stable patients, while recognising that TBI, contusion and multitrauma may alter timing. [R09, R22]

## 6.8 Tracheobronchial injury and bronchopleural fistula

- Tracheobronchial disruption is suspected after severe deceleration, penetrating airway trauma or instrumentation when there is **persistent massive air leak despite an appropriately placed chest drain, failure of lung re-expansion, pneumomediastinum/subcutaneous emphysema, haemoptysis or inability to ventilate effectively**.
- CT may show airway defects, displaced tube or fallen-lung signs, but **bronchoscopy is the diagnostic reference standard** and should guide ETT positioning.
- Positive-pressure ventilation can enlarge the defect and worsen air leak. [R09]

- Initial management is airway control under experienced bronchoscopic guidance, chest drainage, oxygenation and early thoracic surgery.
- Where feasible, position the ETT cuff **distal to a proximal tracheal lesion** or selectively ventilate the unaffected bronchus; a bronchial blocker or double-lumen tube may isolate the affected lung.
- This can be impossible with lesions near the carina, and additional manipulation may worsen injury.
- **Bronchopleural fistula (BPF)** is a communication between bronchial tree and pleura: high airway pressure drives leak, causes loss of tidal volume/PEEP and prevents lung re-expansion.
- Reduce airway pressures and inspiratory time, use the lowest effective PEEP, control infection/drain the pleura, and consider independent lung ventilation or surgical/bronchoscopic closure for major leaks.
- During repair, confirm need for lung isolation and a shared airway plan with the surgeon.
- Avoid confusing a small postoperative alveolopleural leak with a catastrophic central bronchial disruption.

**BPF risk-factor reasoning for the ANZCA Final:**

- A postoperative BPF is especially associated with pneumonectomy (particularly the right side), impaired bronchial-stump blood supply, infection/empyema, persistent positive-pressure ventilation and high airway pressures, malnutrition, diabetes, immunosuppression/steroids, radiation or chemotherapy, and pre-existing pulmonary disease.
- A traumatic fistula follows laceration, airway rupture or bronchial stump disruption.
- For a planned **right-sided fistula repair**, one defensible approach is **left-sided lung isolation** using an appropriate left-sided double-lumen tube (or a single-lumen tube plus bronchial blocker if anatomy and expertise favour it); confirm placement bronchoscopically and minimise pressure transmitted to the fistula.
- For a large or central defect close to the carina, bronchoscopically guided selective intubation of the intact bronchus may be safer than relying on a blocker that cannot seal the fistula.
- Discuss preoxygenation, pre-existing sepsis/air leak, chest-drain function, surgeon access, potential difficulty ventilating a single injured lung and rescue oxygenation strategies.
- The critical exam skill is to **select and justify one airway technique**, not merely list devices (2024.1 examiner report, Q8). [R09]

### Ventilating an established bronchopleural fistula: a pressure-flow problem

- Understand the fistula as an abnormal parallel path between the ventilator and pleural drain.
- The gas volume passing through the fistula increases when the bronchial–pleural pressure gradient, airway peak pressure, inspiratory time or affected-lung exposure increases.
- Therefore a ‘normal’ tidal volume at the ventilator may not reach alveoli; the patient can have severe hypoventilation while circuit flow appears high.
- Compare delivered and expired tidal volume, chest-drain bubbling, ETCO₂ and arterial PaCO₂, and inspect the drainage system for leaks before attributing everything to the lung injury.

- A temporary strategy while bronchoscopy and surgery are arranged is a lower tidal volume, lower peak and plateau pressures, shorter inspiratory time and minimum PEEP that preserves oxygenation; accept some permissive hypercapnia if safe for the patient’s brain and pulmonary circulation.
- Avoid high-frequency or complex rescue techniques without expertise because they may worsen the communication.
- If one bronchial tree can be isolated from the defect, an appropriate DLT, blocker or bronchoscopically positioned single-lumen tube can protect the unaffected lung.
- In a right bronchopleural fistula with an intact left lung, a left-sided DLT or selective left mainstem strategy may be defensible; however, the safest option depends on whether the fistula is proximal, near the carina or distal.
- State how the surgeon and anaesthetist will maintain oxygenation during airway division or cross-field ventilation, and how lung isolation will be confirmed after positioning.
- Post-repair ventilatory pressures should remain low enough to protect the suture line, while preserving gas exchange and avoiding prolonged deep sedation unnecessarily. [R09]

## 6.9 Open pneumothorax, traumatic asphyxia and diaphragmatic injury

- A large open chest-wall wound may cause preferential airflow through the wound rather than the upper airway, impairing ventilation.
- Apply an appropriate **vented chest seal** (or temporarily an occlusive dressing with an escape route, monitoring closely for tension) and insert a chest drain through a separate sterile site before definitive wall repair.
- Traumatic asphyxia from abrupt thoracic compression causes venous hypertension, facial/neck cyanosis, petechiae and subconjunctival haemorrhage; evaluate coexisting thoracic/brain injuries and manage supportively.
- Diaphragmatic rupture after blunt or penetrating thoracoabdominal trauma may cause abdominal viscera in the chest, respiratory compromise and strangulation; CT is useful, but small penetrating defects may need diagnostic laparoscopy/thoracoscopy.
- Repair and pleural drainage are generally indicated. [R09]

items.title: 7. Blunt cardiac injury and traumatic aortic disruption
items.body:
## 7.1 Blunt cardiac injury: why a fractured sternum is not the diagnosis

- A direct blow or rapid deceleration can produce a spectrum from minor myocardial bruising to clinically important myocardial dysfunction, arrhythmia, coronary dissection/thrombosis, valvular or septal rupture and pericardial injury.
- The term **myocardial contusion** is often used loosely; its most clinically important consequences are **dysrhythmia, pump failure and structural disruption**.
- A patient with a fractured sternum and stable haemodynamics may have no significant cardiac lesion.
- Equally, an apparently minor external injury may conceal a coronary injury or chamber rupture.

- The initial evaluation is an **admission 12-lead ECG and troponin** when blunt cardiac injury is suspected.
- An abnormal admission ECG, raised troponin or relevant haemodynamic instability warrants monitoring and repeat assessment.
- **A normal ECG and normal troponin together make clinically significant blunt cardiac injury unlikely**, though timing and assay matter.
- Echocardiography is most valuable with sustained hypotension, new significant arrhythmia, shock unexplained by bleeding or a suspected structural lesion; a normal echo does not exclude every minor contusion.
- **Sternal fracture alone is not an indication for monitoring when ECG and troponin are normal.** Creatine kinase-MB is not a useful screening substitute. [R23]

- Management is physiologically directed.
- Correct hypoxia, hypovolaemia, anaemia and acidosis
- Treat significant arrhythmias according to resuscitation principles
- Use echo to distinguish impaired LV/RV function from haemorrhage or tamponade
- Involve cardiology/cardiothoracic surgery for valve, coronary, septal or chamber injury.
- In unstable patients, select inotropes/vasopressors and fluid based on the identified lesion rather than reflexively giving a large fluid bolus.
- For urgent noncardiac surgery, communicate the monitoring and postoperative disposition plan; a minor troponin elevation alone does not necessarily mandate cancellation of lifesaving surgery.

- **Exam vignette:** After a horse kick or road crash, a patient has sternal bruising but no symptoms. Do not order an indiscriminate echo, serial CK-MB and cardiac CT. Explain why ECG plus troponin are the useful first-screen tests; monitor and investigate further only when results or clinical findings suggest significant injury.

## 7.2 Traumatic thoracic aortic injury: physics and grading

- Rapid deceleration produces shear at relatively fixed aortic segments, classically near the **isthmus distal to the left subclavian artery**; penetrating injury or direct chest trauma may affect other sites.
- Free rupture is usually rapidly fatal.
- Survivors may have a contained intimal lesion, intramural haematoma, pseudoaneurysm or threatened rupture.
- Chest/back pain, pulse asymmetry, abnormal chest radiograph or high-energy mechanism may suggest injury, but a normal CXR is not sufficiently reassuring; **CT angiography** is the first-line diagnostic test in a stable patient. [R09, R24]

The Society for Vascular Surgery (SVS) grading system is commonly:

| **Grade** | **Imaging lesion** | **Management implication (2026 SVS update)** |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | Intimal tear | Definitive nonoperative management; routine follow-up CTA not generally needed if uncomplicated |
| **II** | Intramural haematoma | Definitive nonoperative management with at least one surveillance CTA, commonly at 1–3 months |
| **III** | Pseudoaneurysm | Usually TEVAR; in a stable patient, **delayed >24 h** may be appropriate to manage competing injuries |
| **IV** | Aortic rupture | Emergency repair when feasible |

The **2026 SVS guideline** significantly refines older algorithms: grade I and II are now generally nonoperative, not all grade II lesions require routine TEVAR, and treatment of grade III is often delayed when stable. Instability attributable to aortic bleeding mandates urgent or emergency control. [R24]

## 7.3 Anti-impulse therapy, associated TBI and anaesthesia for TEVAR

- Reducing **aortic dP/dt** (contractility and rate of pressure rise) and systemic pressure lowers shear forces on an injured aorta.
- Where indicated and safe, use titratable **IV beta blockade** (e.g., esmolol) to reduce heart rate before adding vasodilators, aiming for controlled HR/BP rather than abrupt hypotension; often cited targets are **HR approximately 60–80/min and SBP approximately 100–120 mmHg**, individualised to perfusion and associated injuries.
