items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
The College’s Final Examination standard is not merely to reproduce XABCDE or name a drug. Candidates are expected to **reason through priorities, select a treatment and justify it, identify complications and review their clinical response**. The following examples were checked in the uploaded examination reports:

| **Sitting/question** | **What was tested** | **What examiner commentary indicates a complete answer needs** |
|---|---|---|
| **2022.2 Q10** | Role of ultrasound in initial major-trauma assessment | What eFAST detects, where its sensitivity is limited, and how physiology determines whether further imaging or immediate haemorrhage control is appropriate |
| **2023.1 Q2** | Unconscious trauma patient with possible cervical injury | Airway protection **and** cervical protection, not one at the expense of the other; resuscitation and practical airway strategy |
| **2023.2 Q3** | Life-threatening pelvic haemorrhage | Explain pelvic bleeding mechanisms and definitive options; detail haemostatic resuscitation and postoperative care, not merely write “ATLS/MTP” |
| **2024.1 Q8** | BPF risk factors and airway plan | List several risk factors and choose and justify a specific lung/airway isolation strategy accounting for the air leak |
| **2024.1 Q15** | Post-procedure suspected pneumothorax | Clinical severity, exclusion of tension, targeted imaging and management by symptoms/size, plus disclosure and documentation |
| **2025.2 Q10** | Neurogenic shock after high-thoracic SCI | Distinguish from spinal shock and occult bleeding; treat bradycardia/vasoplegia, protect ventilation, name MAP and invasive monitoring strategy |
| **2026.1 MCQ topic list** | Bronchopleural fistula ventilatory strategy | Explain air leak mechanics and why lower airway pressure or lung isolation works rather than naming an arbitrary ventilator mode |

## 17.1 Interpreting trials without overclaiming

| **Trial/guideline** | **Population/intervention** | **Exam-level interpretation** |
|---|---|---|
| **CRASH-2 (2010)** | 20,211 trauma patients with significant bleeding/risk, TXA versus placebo | Lower deaths from bleeding, greatest benefit early; TXA beyond 3 h may be harmful in traumatic haemorrhage |
| **PROPPR (2015)** | 680 severe trauma patients, 1:1:1 vs 1:1:2 plasma:platelets:RBCs | No significant reduction in overall 24-h or 30-day mortality; 1:1:1 improved haemostasis and reduced early exsanguination death |
| **PATCH-Trauma (2023)** | Prehospital TXA vs placebo in trauma patients at risk of coagulopathy | No significant benefit in six-month survival with favourable functional outcome; do not claim unequivocal long-term recovery benefit |
| **UK-REBOA (2023)** | Standard care + REBOA vs standard care in 90 patients with torso exsanguination | High probability of harm; 90-day deaths 54% vs 42%; routinely adding REBOA is not supported as survival-improving |
| **AO Spine/Praxis (2024)** | Review of SCI perfusion and early decompression | MAP 75–80 to 90–95 mmHg for 3–7 days suggested, with very low certainty; early decompression within 24 h where appropriate |
| **WSES–AAST (2025)** | Thoracic-trauma evidence/consensus | Addresses surgical stabilisation (including 48–72 h for suitable cases), bronchial injury, haemothorax and pneumothorax management |
| **SVS (2026)** | Blunt thoracic aortic injury update | Grades I/II usually nonoperative, stable grade III can have delayed TEVAR, grade IV urgent, TBI changes anti-impulse priorities |

- The major trial **does not replace the patient**.
- For example, CRASH-2 supports prompt TXA in traumatic haemorrhage; PATCH asks whether long-term functional recovery improves in advanced systems.
- Both can be true without contradiction.
- Similarly, UK-REBOA caution does not mean every conceivable expert-system deployment in peri-arrest pelvic haemorrhage is always inappropriate; it means the burden of justification is high and delay to definitive haemorrhage control must be avoided.

items.title: Reading list and linked references
items.body:
## Evidence audit and scope

> **Clinical use:** This is an examination teaching resource, not a replacement for current local major-haemorrhage, trauma, airway, chest-drain, spinal clearance, blood-product or medication policies. Numerical targets and indications often differ with associated brain/spinal injury, pregnancy, age, physiology and available expertise. In emergencies, use the institution’s current algorithm and consultant-led multidisciplinary management.

The initial 36-page manuscript was independently re-audited against all 30 workbook-assigned learning-outcome rows, the December 2025 ANZCA curriculum, available Final examiner reports and contemporaneous trauma guidance. The original structure was retained, and gaps were corrected within the relevant teaching chapters. Of the 30 parent outcomes, 27 are scheduled for completion in this set; the other three remain shared outcomes and the relevant components only are addressed here. “Mapped to a chapter” was not accepted as proof of adequate depth: the final audit assessed whether physiology, differential diagnosis, tests, procedural decisions, thresholds and subsequent care were explained.

### 18.2 Independent clinical completeness checks

**Primary survey and imaging:** verified preparation, injury mechanism, history, XABCDE, repeated assessments, eFAST windows/limitations, CXR/CT/CTA selection, and the clinically vital distinction between stable/responding and unstable/nonresponding patients. **Airway/spine:** checked airway indications, physiology of peri-intubation collapse, rescue airway, cervical motion restriction/CT clearance and contraindications to blind tubes. **Haemorrhage:** confirmed bleeding sources, rapid control, MHP, goal-directed coagulation, TXA timing, calcium and hypothermia, permissive hypotension exception in brain/spinal injury, DCS/EDRT/REBOA evidence. **Thorax:** specifically verified every item in SS_TS 1.22—pneumothorax/tension, haemothorax, rib and sternal fracture analgesia, flail chest, contusion, blunt aortic injury, tracheobronchial injury/BPF, thoracostomy, indications for thoracotomy and SSRF. **Abdominal/pelvic/limb:** confirmed organ injury/operative versus nonoperative pathways, pelvic binder/packing/IR options, major vascular injury, fracture immobilisation, compartment/crush and abdominal compartment syndrome. **Neuro/ICU:** verified initial TBI/SCI, neurogenic versus spinal shock, secondary injury prevention, transfer, analgesia and ICU surveillance.

This independent review checked emergency procedural detail, the 2023/2025 European and Australian critical-bleeding guidance, ANZCA 2024.2 ESP-block examiner expectations, 2022.2 ultrasound examiner feedback, the 2023.2 pelvic-haemorrhage examiner report, the 2025.2 neurogenic-shock report, WSES–AAST 2025 chest guidance, SVS 2026 BTAI recommendations and the relevant BJA Education and 2025 ANZCA Blue Book material. The more consequential omissions were corrected in their natural positions: imaging interpretation and ultrasound limitations; drug and coagulation targets; actual chest-drain and rib-block procedure detail; definitive haemorrhage control; and ICU course. Numerical values are identified as conditional where the guideline evidence is limited or local products differ.

**Limits of what a written note set can certify:** actual skill in thoracostomy, major-haemorrhage teamwork, difficult airway management and resuscitative thoracotomy depends on supervised training, simulation, local protocols and workplace assessment. The examination reports uploaded to this project are available for selected sittings from 2015.2 to 2026.1; they do not establish a complete historical SAQ-bank mapping back to 2006. Exact examiner-based SAQ model answers/self-marking belong in the separate Retrieve/SAQ/Speak resources rather than being confused with the textbook teaching document.

### 18.3 Audit findings integrated into the teaching

After a second pass, the original work was judged broadly clinically sound but not adequately detailed for a standalone FEx learning resource in five high-stakes areas: trauma imaging interpretation, operational major haemorrhage/goal-directed coagulation, practical thoracic procedures, procedural rib-fracture regional analgesia, and definitive pelvic/abdominal haemorrhage pathways. Those gaps have now been addressed in the chapters above, not in an appended disconnected fact list. The remaining unavoidable limitation is that examination outcomes include procedural competence and real-time team leadership that cannot be certified by reading a document. Local policies for chest drains, MHP, anticoagulant reversal and regional blocks take precedence for patients.

## Recommended reading sequence

- **1.** **Gordon, Naumann & Shilston (2025), Early intensive care management of major trauma in adults,** [part 1](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.10.003)**and** [part 2](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.08.005)**:** first-pass ICU physiology, ventilatory priorities, haemorrhage and abdominal damage-control decisions.
- **2.** **Mockridge & Turner (2025),** [Prehospital management of the airway in trauma](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.05.002)**:** physiologically and anatomically difficult airways, high-quality first attempt, spinal precautions and failed-intubation planning.
- **3.** [Anaesthetic management of abdominal trauma](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.09.005)**(BJA Education, 2025):** DCR and damage-control surgery, anaesthesia at laparotomy and transition to ICU care.
- **4.** [Anaesthetic and surgical management of rib fractures](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2020.06.001)**(BJA Education, 2020):** multimodal/regional analgesia, contusion and ventilation, indications for fixation.
- **5.** **ANZCA Australasian Anaesthesia 2025,** [Goal-directed bleeding management: Understanding and implementing viscoelastic haemostatic assays across patient blood management](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1387)**:** physiological and VHA/ROTEM/TEG interpretation for active bleeding; identify when empiric ratios should become targeted treatment.
- **6.** **ANZCA Australasian Anaesthesia 2025,** [B-lines and beyond: Lung ultrasound for the perioperative clinician](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1305)**and The emergency laparotomy patient (same volume):** applied bedside ultrasound and high-risk abdominal surgery physiology. These are supplemental articles; an emergency laparotomy review should not be substituted for trauma-specific operative management.

## Linked guidelines and key references

The links below identify the externally checked public sources. The ANZCA December 2025 curriculum, the Set 7 workbook and the uploaded Chair’s reports are the **primary curriculum and examination mapping sources**; public guidance is used to update the clinical teaching. References apply to the specific topics cited in the body, not as blanket endorsement of every management choice.

### Evidence hierarchy and practical caveats

The **ANZCA curriculum sets what is examinable**; examiner reports show where clinically plausible but superficial answers fail. Contemporary professional guidelines inform current practice, but a clinical guideline can contain consensus recommendations of low certainty; this is labelled where significant. RCT evidence is preferred for claims of outcome benefit, while observational studies and expert consensus underpin some emergency procedures and thresholds. The notes intentionally distinguish **what is proven to improve outcomes** from **reasonable first-line practice** and **context-dependent expert decisions**. For actual patients, follow the contemporaneous institutional algorithm, discuss conflicts between recommendations and maintain a senior multidisciplinary decision-making framework.
